newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke proves his mettle to the markets.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke proves his mettle to the markets.

text.p: When Kenneth Clarke became Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer in May 1993, financial markets were concerned he would cut interest rates as low as possible to keep voters loyal to the ruling Conservative party.

But on Wednesday, he broke with decades of political tradition by raising the cost of borrowing just months ahead of the next general election, due by May 1997. The quarter point rise took rates to 6.0 percent.

While Clarke was undoubtedly mindful of an increasingly vocal central bank pushing for a rate rise, he was almost certainly convinced by Britain's long run of strong economic data and early warning signals on inflation.

"Clarke was convinced by his Treasury advisers and the economic evidence that an upward move was necessary...he was not forced into it by the central bank," said Richard Jeffrey, economist at Charterhouse Tilney in London.
Economic growth, at 2.3 percent in the third quarter and set to climb to three or four percent in 1997, is way above the 2.25 percent annual growth over the past 40 years.

And with core inflation at 2.9 percent against a government target of 2.5 percent or lower, Clarke's action was dictated by the anti-inflation framework put in place after sterling was ejected from Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.

"The weight of evidence indicated that, without some rapid monetary tightening, the Chancellor was in danger of both missing his inflation target and losing some hard won credibility. This helps on both counts," said Jeremy Peat, chief economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.
But analysts said it was too early to say Clarke would meet his demanding -- at least by British standards -- inflation target by the end of the current parliament.
"But he (Clarke) is obviously committed to sound economic management. The days of 80s-style slash and burn economics are long gone," said Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Many economists are concerned, however, that British consumers are rediscovering their dangerous borrowing and spending ways of the 1980s boom, as retail sales volumes rise around four percent year-on-year and consumer credit jumps.
The rate rise was the first since February 1995 and since then there had been four quarter point reductions, with the latest cut -- opposed by the central bank -- in June.
But it would be churlish to see the latest rise as a U-turn, as Clarke is trying to fine-tune policy with quarter point moves, avoiding the big monetary shocks of the 1970s and 1980s.

Many Conservative members of Parliament will, no doubt, complain the rate rise will alienate voters with big home loans to pay. In a country where 67 percent buy their own homes, the state of the housing market is political dynamite.

But economists said Clarke's action could avoid sharper rises in the cost of borrowing later, either at the November 26 budget or closer to the election, which could prove much more painful politically.

Clarke has made it crystal clear to his detractors -- mostly on the right-wing of the Conservative party -- that only by prudent stewardship of the economy can they hope to regain the electoral initiative from Labour, and that there are no short-cuts to economic or poll success.
And economists said Clarke had to tighten monetary policy now to allow any easing at all of tax rates in the budget.

"Tactically it was a shrewd move. Clarke had to rebalance monetary policy to prepare the ground for the expected tax cuts. He also knew he would have to tighten at some stage ahead of the election, and he decided earlier was better than later," said David Coleman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Britons are still paying higher taxes imposed after the 1990-92 recession which pushed up government borrowing sharply. Lower taxes, combined with cheap home loans, are widely seen as the tonic to tempt voters back to the Conservatives, who trail the opposition Labour party by 15 to 20 percent in the polls.

But despite the rate rise any tax giveaway is likely to be limited to a penny off the basic 24 pence in the pound tax rate, as Britain's borrowing requirement -- the gap between government spending and borrowing -- is forecast by the Treasury to fall to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, just making the target laid down by the Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union.
Clever stewardship of the economy and tax cuts may not be enough, however, to help Clarke and the Conservatives out of their current electoral rut.

A Reuter poll of 20 top political forecasters, published on Wednesday, showed 19 expected Labour to win the next general election, a clear warning that the Conservatives have an electoral mountain to climb to win a fifth consecutive poll.
